title: Nelson Mandela: Long Walk to Freedom + A Tiger in the Zoo — Chapter Summary
intro: Chapter 2 of First Flight pairs an excerpt from Nelson Mandela's autobiography 'Long Walk to Freedom' with Leslie Norris's poem 'A Tiger in the Zoo'. Both explore FREEDOM from opposite poles — Mandela from the side of new political freedom on the day of his inauguration as South Africa's first black President (10 May 1994), and Norris from the side of ongoing captivity through the eye of a caged tiger. Together they teach us that freedom is INDIVISIBLE — winning it takes generations; losing it diminishes even the captor.

sections.heading: Mandela's Inauguration
bullets: 10 May 1994 — Mandela inaugurated as first black President of South Africa.
Held at the Union Buildings sandstone amphitheatre in Pretoria.
Mandela's daughter Zenani and his deputies F.W. de Klerk and Thabo Mbeki on stage.
New flag raised; African anthem 'Nkosi Sikelel' iAfrika' sung; Air Force fly-past.
Three centuries of white rule — and 46 years of formal apartheid — formally end.

sections.heading: What Mandela Said — Key Ideas
bullets: Apartheid was 'an extraordinary human disaster' — 'a deep and lasting wound'.
'Never, never and never again shall it be that this beautiful land will again experience the oppression of one by another.'
Twin obligations of every person — to FAMILY and to PEOPLE.
'Courage was not the absence of fear, but the triumph over it.'
'No one is born hating... if they can learn to hate, they can be taught to love'.
Three stages of freedom — boy's freedom of village; young man's right to dignity; adult's understanding that all must be free.

sections.heading: Background of Apartheid
bullets: Apartheid (Afrikaans: 'separateness') was the official policy from 1948.
Black Africans, coloured people and Indians were denied vote, dignified work, good education, equal access to public spaces.
Mandela joined the ANC, was sentenced to life imprisonment in 1964 and held mostly on Robben Island for 27 years.
International pressure + internal resistance forced negotiation; Mandela released 1990; apartheid laws repealed 1991.
First multi-racial democratic election: 27 April 1994; ANC won; Mandela inaugurated 10 May 1994.

sections.heading: A Tiger in the Zoo — Form and Plot
bullets: Leslie Norris's 1969 poem; five stanzas of four lines each.
Rhyme scheme: ABCB (2nd and 4th lines rhyme).
Stanzas alternate: caged tiger / wild tiger / caged tiger / wild tiger / caged tiger at night.
Caged: paces on pads of velvet, ignores visitors, watches the stars.
Wild: slides through long grass, lurks near a water-hole, snarls near a village.
Final image: tiger stares at the brilliant stars — an unreachable freedom.

sections.heading: Themes — A Tiger in the Zoo
bullets: Freedom and captivity — the contrast as the poem's argument.
Nature vs human-made world — wild scenes are the tiger's true element.
Dignity in captivity — he ignores visitors, paces with care.
Cruelty of zoos — an indirect critique through image.
A small mirror of Mandela — the prisoner's gaze at distant freedom.

sections.heading: What Unifies the Chapter
bullets: Both pieces explore FREEDOM from opposite poles.
Mandela from new freedom; Norris from ongoing captivity.
Mandela's voice — calm, public, factual; Norris's — quiet, intimate, image-based.
Mandela's insight that 'the oppressor is as unfree as the oppressed' echoes in the tiger poem.
Together: freedom is indivisible — at the scale of a nation and at the scale of a single creature.

key_takeaways: Mandela was inaugurated as South Africa's first black President on 10 May 1994 — ending three centuries of white rule.
Apartheid (Afrikaans 'separateness') was the official policy from 1948 to 1991.
Mandela spent 27 years in prison, mostly on Robben Island, before being released in 1990.
Mandela's twin obligations: to family and to people; under apartheid, both were impossible to fulfil.
Courage = triumph over fear. Love comes more naturally to the human heart than hate.
Mandela's deepest insight: no one is free until all are free; the oppressor is as unfree as the oppressed.
Leslie Norris's poem alternates caged and wild scenes to show what is lost when a wild creature is caged.
Together, Mandela's prose and Norris's poem make freedom — and its loss — vividly real at every scale.

The ability to recover from hardship and continue.
